beginner: The most common pea-shoot problem. In wet, crowded, stuffy conditions, tiny fungi rot the baby plants at the base, and you often see fuzzy white or gray mold on the surface. A thick layer of soaked pea seeds holds a lot of water, so it molds easily if the air is still.
seasoned: Soil-borne fungi (Rhizoctonia, Botrytis, and others) rot seedlings at the soil line under wet, crowded, still conditions, often alongside fuzzy white or gray surface mold. It is the number-one pea-shoot failure, and the dense mat of large soaked seeds is unusually prone: it traps moisture, stays humid, and mats down airflow.

beginner: You cannot spray this away on a crop you eat raw, so the fix is prevention: drain the soaked seed well, keep the mix just damp (not soggy), water from the bottom once the leaves are up, keep a small fan running, do not pile the seed on too thick, and clean your trays between batches. If a tray molds badly, toss it and start over with clean equipment.
seasoned: Prevention is the whole game: drain the soaked seed well before sowing, keep the medium at wrung-sponge moisture, bottom-water once greened, run constant gentle airflow, sow a sensible (not overwhelming) rate, and sanitize trays between cycles. beginner: Pea shoots follow five steps: soak, plant, keep dark, give light, then harvest. Soak the peas overnight (about 8 to 12 hours), keep the covered tray warm (around 70 °F) and dark for about three days while they sprout, then uncover into bright light (about 68 to 72 °F) for roughly 18 hours a day until they green up. They are usually ready in 10 to 16 days, a little later than tiny microgreens like radish. If you cut above the lowest little leaf, you may get a smaller second cutting about a week later.
seasoned: The cycle is presoak, sow, blackout, light, harvest. Soak the large seed about 8 to 12 hours, then germinate at about 70 °F under a weighted cover in the dark for roughly 3 days, uncover into about 18 hours of light at 68 to 72 °F to green up, then cut at about 4 to 6 inches when tendrils and the first true leaves show. Most trays finish in 10 to 16 days, a bit later than small brassica microgreens; a shorter cotyledon-stage cut can be taken nearer 8 to 10 days. Cutting above the lowest node can yield a lighter, coarser second flush a week or so later.

beginner: To always have pea shoots ready, start a new tray every week or so instead of one big batch. Because they grow indoors, you can keep this going all year. Just remember to soak the next batch of peas the night before you plant.
seasoned: For a steady supply, stagger sowings: start a fresh tray every 5 to 7 days rather than one big tray at once. Indoors there is no season, so the cadence is limited only by your tray count and counter space. Remember to start the presoak the night before each sow.

beginner: Pea shoots are baby pea plants that you grow indoors and harvest young, about 10 to 16 days after planting, when they are a few inches tall with curling tendrils. They taste sweet and fresh, like a snap pea, and are more tender and a little taller than tiny microgreens like radish. The big pea seed makes them easy but has one special step: you soak the peas overnight (about 8 to 12 hours) before planting them thickly on a shallow tray of seed-starting mix or a growing mat. Then you cover the tray to keep it dark for a few days while they sprout, move it into the light to green up, and snip them off. There is no outdoor season or weather to worry about, so they grow the same way no matter where you live.
seasoned: Pea shoots are the young seedlings of the garden pea (Pisum sativum), grown indoors as a tall, sweet microgreen and cut at about 4 to 6 inches when the tendrils and first true leaves appear, roughly 10 to 16 days after sowing. The large seed is the whole story: it must be presoaked about 8 to 12 hours before a heavy, dense sow, it carries enough food to reach harvest without fertilizer, and its bulk gives shoots that are taller, sweeter, and sturdier than tiny brassica microgreens. The cycle is presoak, then a dense sow on a shallow tray of mix or a fiber mat, a short dark blackout under a weight to even the stand and shed seed coats, then light to green up, then cut. Because there is no frost, season, or hardiness zone involved, the same tray grows identically on a windowsill anywhere.

beginner: Your pea shoots are ready when they are about 4 to 6 inches tall with little curling tendrils and the first true leaves, usually 10 to 16 days after planting. Snip them just above the soil with clean scissors and eat them fresh. If you instead cut a bit higher, above the lowest little leaf, the plants may grow a smaller second batch about a week later, though it will not be as nice as the first.
seasoned: Cut at about 4 to 6 inches, when the tendrils and first true leaves have appeared, typically 10 to 16 days from sowing (a shorter cotyledon-stage cut can be taken nearer 8 to 10 days). Snip just above the medium with clean scissors. Cutting instead just above the lowest node or leaf can leave the plant to push a lighter, coarser second flush about a week later, but the main tray is best treated as a single cut.
